title: Race Operations
subtitle: Meetings, entries, declarations, race day and certified results
summary: Race Operations runs the racing programme: meetings on open calendar days, races with distance, surface and purse, entries checked live against the Horse Registry and Participants, field declaration with the draw, scratchings, race officials, and results that become immutable once certified.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Every entry triggers three live checks: is the horse eligible on race day (Horse Registry), does the jockey hold a valid JOCKEY licence (Participants), and who trains the horse (Participants). The entry fee is charged to the horse's largest owner on race day.

Declaring the field draws the barriers and commits the purse to the GL (PURSE_COMMITMENT). Starting a race tells Wagering to close its pools; certifying the result makes it OFFICIAL, which is the signal Wagering and Prizes wait for before paying anybody.
A cancelled race releases its purse and voids its pools, with refunds handled by Wagering.

sections.title: Race Operations database architecture · Visual ERD
sections.intro: The racing_operations schema defines five tables and nine declared foreign keys. It connects a race meeting to individual races, entries, officials and certified results, while referencing Venue, Horse and Party master data from other schemas.

sections.title: Nine foreign-key relationships in plain English
rows: This meeting takes place at a known club venue.
Every race belongs to one meeting.
Every entry belongs to a race.
The declared runner exists in the horse master.
The optional jockey reference is an existing Party record.
The optional trainer reference is an existing Party record.
One entry may have at most one recorded result.
The official serves a particular race.
The official must exist as a Party.

sections.title: What MySQL guarantees—and what business services must enforce
items: SQL guarantees: a race belongs to an existing meeting; an entry to an existing race; referenced horses, parties and venues exist; duplicate horse entries in one race are blocked by UNIQUE(race_id, horse_id).
SQL also guarantees: positive race distances, nonnegative purses, positive recorded finishing positions when present, and a single race_result per race_entry.

Race-day service rules are separate: the database does not ensure a venue is open, the horse is medically eligible, the jockey has a valid licence on the date, or that a trainer assignment is in force. Those require domain checks.

Certification is a business transition: DDL defines statuses and official_at, but does not itself make an OFFICIAL race result immutable. Application rules or guard triggers must enforce that behavior.
Concurrency matters: version_no supports optimistic-locking patterns; the application must use the field properly when several operators work on the same race.
Finance integration matters: only committed, validated business events should flow to wagering, prize settlement and accounting; downstream processing needs reliable deduplication.

terms.definition: A race day at a venue: PLANNED → OPEN (card published) → COMPLETED.
Number, name, start time, distance, surface, purse, min / max runners. SCHEDULED → DECLARED → RUNNING → OFFICIAL, or CANCELLED.
Horse, jockey, trainer, weight, saddlecloth and (after declaration) draw. Can be scratched before the cutoff.
Finishing positions and times marked official. A database guard forbids any later change.

sections.title: Design decisions
items: Synchronous checks where correctness matters at the moment of entry; asynchronous events where it does not.
Results are immutable after certification: everything downstream (dividends, prize money) depends on them.
Race times are stored as venue wall-clock time; system timestamps are UTC.
